General settings

The General tab of the Admin Console — installation-wide basics (environment badge, default platform, timezone), the bug-report opt-in, the System Information inventory, the per-package Libraries updater, the System packages installer, Update sources (where update packages and Python libraries come from) and the Services card that starts, stops and restarts this node's units.

🔑 Permissionsusers.manage
📍 WhereSettings → System → General (URL /settings/#tab-general)

What is it?#

General is the first tab of the Admin Console (Settings → System → General). It holds the installation-wide basics — environment, default appliance platform, timezone — and three operational cards: System Information with its Libraries updater, and Services, which starts, stops and restarts the units this node runs without giving anyone a shell.

What does it do?#

  • General Configuration form — stores a handful of installation-wide values in the replicated app_settings table (one value for every node of an HA pair).
  • Bug report notifications — a personal opt-in: whether you receive bug reports filed by users (bell + email).
  • System Information — read-only inventory: version, database, Python, operating system and the versions of the tracked libraries.
  • Libraries — checks PyPI for newer versions of the tracked libraries and queues a per-package upgrade or rollback from a curated allowlist. It moves Python dependencies only; the application code is moved by Software update.
  • Services — one section per node with the state of each controllable unit and the Start / Stop / Restart buttons the unit's policy allows.
  • System packages — the operating-system packages SATOM depends on (today bubblewrap, the sandbox for integration hooks, the Python Console and the Script Library), one column per node: ok (installed and the sandbox works for the service account), installed, not usable (the kernel forbids namespaces for that account; the reason is shown), missing or unreachable. Install queues the package for the privileged updater on this node and, if you choose, on the peers. The list is curated and install-only.
  • Update sources — where this installation looks for updates: the update packages feed that Software update reads, and the Python libraries index the Libraries card checks and installs from. Each is Default or a custom https:// URL (an internal pipeline or mirror), public or with a user + token. The index covers Python (pip) libraries only; operating-system packages keep coming from the OS repositories.

Requirements#

  • An account whose profile grants users.manage.
  • Libraries and Services act through the privileged updater service of each node. On a container (Docker) installation, Services shows the stack's containers when the operations agent is present and nothing otherwise; library changes are refused there because packages are baked into the image (see Container operations).

Permissions#

🔑Permission

Every route behind this tab requires users.manage (legacy coarse key user_manage). Users without it do not see the System group in the Settings menu at all, and a direct POST to /settings/general, /settings/services/action or /settings/library-pip returns 403 Forbidden. Typical holder: Administrator.

The Bug report notifications card posts to /reports/prefs/notify, which is also gated on user_manage.

How to use#

Change the general configuration#

  1. Open Settings → System → General.
  2. Edit the fields of the General Configuration card (see Configuration).
  3. Click Save General Settings. The page reloads on the General tab with "General settings saved."

Opt in to bug-report notifications#

  1. In the Bug report notifications card, switch on Receive bug reports from users (bell + email).
  2. Click Save preference. The flash reads "Notification preference saved."

The preference is personal (stored per user), default off.

Check for and apply library updates#

  1. In System Information → Libraries, click Check for updates. This is the only control that contacts PyPI (https://pypi.org); results are cached for 6 hours and the button forces a fresh check. The line under the heading then reads "All tracked libraries up to date · source pypi.org · checked …" or counts the outdated ones. A library PyPI did not answer for shows not checked, never a green tick, and the line says how many went unchecked. Upgrade and Rollback run pip in /opt/satom/venv. With an index set in Update sources, the check and the install both use it and the line names it; otherwise they use pypi.org (pip's own configuration for the install). The job log has a package index step saying where the change installed from.
  2. A library with a newer version shows Upgrade → x.y.z; one with a recorded rollback point shows Rollback → x.y.z.
  3. On an HA pair, tick Also apply on the peer node(s) if the change should be queued on the other node too. It is off by default, so you can stage a risky upgrade on one node first.
  4. Confirm the dialog. The output box shows queued (<id>) on <node> — applying… and then the runner's steps as it installs, smoke-tests and restarts.
  5. With more than one node, a drift table shows each node's installed version and one of: Nodes are level — every curated library matches, Version DRIFT between nodes, or Pair state UNKNOWN — … when a peer did not answer.

Install a missing system package#

  1. In System Information, under Libraries, find System packages. Each node has a column; a package that is not ok on every node shows an Install button.
  2. Click Install. With more than one node you are asked whether to install on all nodes (OK) or on this node only.
  3. The log box follows this node's install: the package manager it used (apt, dnf/yum, zypper or pacman), the install itself and a final sandbox works for satom check. A peer's own updater applies the request there; click Refresh to see its result.

Choose where updates come from#

  1. Scroll to Update sources (under System Information). It has two columns, Update packages and Python libraries, and each is set on its own: you can change one and leave the other on Default.
  2. Set Source to Custom URL and enter the https:// URL: - Update packages: a latest.json in the same format as the public feed, for example https://pipeline.example.com/satom/latest.json. - Python libraries: a pip "simple" index, the URL you would give pip as --index-url, for example https://nexus.example.com/repository/pypi/simple (Nexus, Artifactory, devpi, a GitLab or Gitea package registry, or pypi.org itself).
  3. Set Authentication to None — public URL, or to User + token and fill both. For a token-only service, use the user name its documentation gives for token access (for example __token__ on PyPI-compatible registries).
  4. Click Test. It reaches the source as typed, saved or not, and answers "the feed offers x.y.z (satom-update-x.y.z.tar.gz)" or "the index answers: latest Flask is x.y.z", or the reason it failed.
  5. Click Save. The line reads "Saved. In use: …". Saving a new index re-runs the Libraries check against it. To keep the stored token, leave the token field blank.

To go back, set Source to Default and save: the URL, the user and the token are cleared.

ℹ️Note

The token is write-only. It is stored like every other credential (in the vault at updates/feed or updates/index when one is configured, encrypted locally otherwise) and is never sent back to the page or written to the audit log. It goes only to the URL's own host and never follows a redirect, and pip receives it through its environment, never a command line.

⚠️Warning

Changing the source does not change what the node trusts. An update package from an internal pipeline must still be signed by a key in this node's trust store. A pipeline that republishes the signed packages works as is; one that builds its own needs its key added to the trust store (see Software update).

Start, stop or restart a service#

  1. Scroll to Services. The first section is this node; each registered peer gets its own section, loaded separately so a dead standby never makes this node's card look broken.
  2. Click the action button on the unit's row and confirm. Buttons are state-aware: a running unit offers Restart and (if permitted) Stop; a stopped unit offers Start, or Restart when restart is its only permitted action.
  3. The log box under the table follows the request until the runner reports the outcome.
  4. Click Refresh to re-read every unit's state.

Configuration#

General Configuration card#

Field Description Required Example
Application Name Free text. Stored and shown in System Information and on the profile page. Default SATOM; a blank value is saved as SATOM. See the note below on what it does not change. No SATOM
Environment Production or Development. Drives the PROD/DEV badge in the top bar and on the ADOM picker. Replicated, so both HA nodes agree. Default Development; any other value is stored as development. No Production
Default Appliance Platform Platform pre-selected when registering a new appliance. The choices come from the ADOM registry; an invalid value is normalised to fortiweb (or the first registered platform). Default fortiweb. No FortiWeb
Timezone IANA timezone used to display log and audit timestamps everywhere in the UI, and to interpret times typed into forms (for example maintenance windows and the backup hour). Default Europe/Zurich; an unknown name falls back to the default. No Europe/Berlin
Session Lock (minutes) Idle timeout of a browser session, clamped to 5–1440; default 60. A session with no user activity for this long is signed out on its next request. See Session Lock. No 60
Log Format How lines are written to the application log file (data/logs/satom.log): Plain text (time · level — message), Detailed (timestamp · level · logger · message) or JSON (structured, one object per line). Every format keeps the timestamp. Default plain. Applied on save. No Detailed
Log Levels Which severities are written to the application log: tick any of DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR. Unset means all four; saving with none ticked stores INFO, WARNING, ERROR. Applied on save. No INFO, WARNING, ERROR

Application Name is shown only in System Information and on the profile page; the browser title and top bar show the product name. Environment, Default Appliance Platform, Timezone, Session Lock, Log Format and Log Levels take effect for the whole application: the log settings are applied at start-up and immediately on save, and the Session Lock from the next request.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: Session Lock is enforced as an idle timeout, Log Format and Log Levels are applied to the application log, and the Status Poll Interval and Show raw JSON config fields were removed because nothing read them.

Session Lock#

  • Page loads, Turbo navigation and every form submission count as activity.
  • Background refreshes do not count: the notification bell, job progress, status badges, edit-lock heartbeats and other timed panel reloads. A tab left open therefore still locks.
  • When the timeout has passed, the next request signs the session out and returns to the login page with "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity."; a script call gets a JSON 401 with session_locked: true. The lock is recorded in the Audit Log as session.idle_lock.
  • Requests authenticated with an API token (Bearer) have no session and are never locked.

Services card — what each unit allows#

Unit Label Actions permitted
satom.service Web application Restart
satom-scheduler.service Scheduler Start, Stop, Restart
satom-reconciler.service HA reconciler Start, Stop, Restart
satom-metrics.service Metrics store Start, Stop, Restart
satom-alerts.timer Alert engine (timer) Start, Stop, Restart
satom-cert-renew.timer Certificate renewal (timer) Start, Stop, Restart
satom-ha-datasync.timer HA data sync (timer) Start, Stop, Restart
nginx.service Web front (nginx) Start, Restart (reload is permitted for internal use, never drawn)
postgresql.service PostgreSQL Restart

The updater itself (satom-updater.service, satom-updater.path) is explicitly forbidden: it is the component that applies these requests. Nothing is enabled or disabled — start and stop are runtime-only, and the At boot column shows what the node arms at boot. A unit that is not installed on the node is shown greyed, with no buttons.

Example#

🧪Example — Stage a library upgrade on one node of an HA pair

  1. Open General on the primary and click Check for updates.
  2. Jinja2 shows Upgrade → 3.1.6. Leave Also apply on the peer node(s) unticked.
  3. Confirm; watch the runner install, smoke-test and restart the web application.
  4. The drift table now reads Version DRIFT between nodes. After a day of normal use, open General again, tick the peer box and upgrade — the table returns to Nodes are level.

Result#

  • Saving the form writes the general.* keys and an audit entry settings.general.
  • A service action writes settings.service_action (or settings.service_action.peer); a library change writes settings.library_pip with the package, version, node and peer states.
  • Restarting the web application kills the worker that served your click; the page reconnects and shows the runner's final log, including the health check.

Troubleshooting#

"Failed to save settings: …"#

Possible causes - The database rejected the write (for example a read-only standby node).

Solution 1. Make the change on the primary node; settings replicate to the standby.

Verification — the flash reads "General settings saved." and System Information shows the new values.

"Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity."#

Possible causes - The browser session had no user activity for longer than Session Lock. Background refreshes do not keep a session alive.

Solution 1. Sign in again; you return to the page you requested. 2. If the timeout is too short for your team, raise Session Lock (minutes) (up to 1440).

Verification — the audit log shows session.idle_lock with the idle and configured minutes.

"package '…' is not in the curated allowlist"#

Possible causes - The request named a package that is not on this node's curated list (the list is enforced by the web worker and again by the privileged runner).

Solution — only the packages shown in the Libraries table can be changed from here.

"installed, but satom cannot create namespaces: …"#

Possible causes - bwrap: No permissions to create new namespace (or similar): the kernel or the container does not let the service account create user namespaces (an LXC without nesting, or a sysctl such as kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0). - bwrap: execvp /usr/bin/true: No such file or directory on SLES / openSUSE Leap 15: SATOM versions before the SA-0002 fix assumed a usr-merged system and hid the real /lib64, which holds the program loader on SUSE 15.

Solution — for the first, allow user namespaces for the node and click Install again (an installed package only re-runs the check). For the second, update SATOM; the sandbox now mounts /bin, /sbin, /lib and /lib64 read-only exactly as the host has them, and the card turns ok without reinstalling the package.

"pypi.org is not reachable from this node: versions were NOT checked"#

Possible causes — this node has no route to pypi.org: an offline (air-gapped) install, a proxy, or no DNS. No version was compared, so the card offers no Upgrade.

Solution — on an offline node this is expected: its libraries move with the signed update package (Software Update & HA, see Offline updates). Each package carries the wheels for that release's requirements.txt and installs them with --no-index, so applying it brings every library to the version the release pins. On a node that should be online, check outbound HTTPS. The rest of the page is unaffected because the check never runs during page render; page loads reuse the unreachable result for 10 minutes and the button always retries.

"… cannot be used: the token is stored in the vault, which could not be read: …"#

Possible causes — an update source is set with a user and token, but the token cannot be read (the vault is sealed or unreachable, or the local key changed).

Solution — fix the vault (Settings → Vault → Test connection), or save the source again with the token. SATOM refuses the check, the download and the library change until then; it never falls back to the public default without saying so.

"HTTP 401: the index wants credentials, or refused the ones given"#

Possible causes — the source needs authentication and none was given, or the user or token was rejected. A token without the registry's package-read permission fails the same way.

Solution — set User + token, check the token's scopes on the registry, and click Test again.

"the index answered but lists no release of Flask: …"#

The index answered HTTP 200, but not with a page listing Flask releases. The message goes on to say what did answer — the final URL, its content type, a redirect if there was one — and which of these it is:

The message continues with What it means Solution
redirected from … + a sign-in page the index sits behind a login (SSO, a proxy portal) and SATOM was sent there give SATOM a User + token the index accepts, or exempt the index path from the portal
the page has no download links (title …) — not a package index page the URL is the product's front page or a folder, not the Simple API use the pip URL, which normally ends in /simple: Nexus …/repository/<repo>/simple, Artifactory …/artifactory/api/pypi/<repo>/simple, devpi …/<user>/<index>/+simple, GitLab …/packages/pypi/simple
JSON that is not the Simple API (keys: …) the server answered with its own JSON API, and asking again for HTML did not help same as above: point at the Simple API URL
N link(s), none of them a Flask distribution file a private registry that only holds your own packages add a PyPI proxy (or a group that includes one) to the registry and point SATOM at it
only yanked or pre-release files of Flask the mirror is incomplete sync the mirror

"Update check failed: SATOM did not answer the request."#

Possible causes — the check endpoint itself failed (the web service was restarting, or the session expired).

Solution — reload the page and click Check for updates again.

A Services action says "… is not allowed on '…' from this console"#

Possible causes — the action is not in the unit's policy (for example Stop on the web application, nginx or PostgreSQL).

Solution — use Restart, or act from a shell if you really need to stop the unit.

"could not queue: …"#

Possible causes — the request directory for the privileged runner is not writable, or the runner is not installed.

Solution — check the updater units with the CLI and the services and timers reference.

Advanced#

Advanced Where things are stored and how requests run
  • General values live in app_settings under general.app_name, general.env_mode, general.default_kind, general.timezone, general.session_timeout, general.log_format and general.log_levels (JSON list). The former general.poll_interval and general.show_raw_config keys may still exist in the table; nothing reads or writes them.
  • The Session Lock value is cached for 30 seconds per worker and the cache is cleared on save. The last-activity time is stored in the signed session cookie.
  • The bug-report opt-in is a per-user setting, default "0".
  • The web worker never runs pip or systemctl. It writes a JSON request that the root-owned updater applies; the browser polls /settings/services/status/<id> or /settings/library-pip/status/<id>.
  • Peer actions go to the other node's /settings/peer/* endpoints, authenticated by a request signature made with the shared node identity key (not a user session; the key itself is never sent). The peer re-validates the unit or package against its own allowlist. Without a configured key the peer answers node identity key not configured (503); with a missing, wrong or stale signature (clocks more than 120 seconds apart) bad node key (403).
  • The library update check caches results in-process for 6 hours.
